'''Gustav Arnold Hedlund''' (May 7, 1904 – March 15, 1993), an American [[mathematician]], was one of the founders of [[symbolic dynamics|symbolic]] and [[topological dynamics]].

==Biography==
Hedlund was born May 7, 1904, in [[Somerville, Massachusetts]]. He did his undergraduate studies at [[Harvard University]], earned a master's degree from [[Columbia University]], and returned to Harvard for his doctoral studies. He was a student of [[Marston Morse]], under whose supervision he received a Ph.D. in 1930 with thesis entitled "I. Geodesics on a Two-Dimensional Riemannian Manifold with Periodic Coefficients II. Poincare's Rotation Number and Morse's Type Number".<ref name="citation">{{citation
 | contribution = Citation read to the Faculty of Graduate School of Yale University on the occasion of Professor Hedlund's retirement
 | editor-last = Beck | editor-first = Anatole
 | location = Berlin
 | mr = 0370654
 | page = viii+285
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | series = Lecture Notes in Mathematics, Vol. 318
 | title = Proceedings of the Conference on Topological Dynamics held at Yale University on August 23, 1972, in honor of Professor Gustav Arnold Hedlund on the occasion of his retirement
 | year = 1973}}.</ref><ref name="briscoe">[http://www.lib.utexas.edu/taro/utcah/01645/01645-P.html G. A. Hedlund Papers, 1941-1945, 2008], Dolph Briscoe Center for American History, The University of Texas at Austin, retrieved 2011-09-10.</ref><ref name="mg">{{mathgenealogy|name=Gustav Arnold Hedlund|id=6968}}.</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Poincaré's rotational number and Morse's type number|journal=Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1932|volume=34|issue=1|pages=75–97|mr=1501630|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/tran/1932-034-01/S0002-9947-1932-1501630-8/S0002-9947-1932-1501630-8.pdf|doi=10.2307/1989503|jstor=1989503|last1=Hedlund|first1=Gustav A.}}</ref>

While still studying at Columbia, Hedlund taught at [[Hunter College]], and after receiving his doctorate he took a position at [[Bryn Mawr College]], where he remained for nine years. From 1939 to 1948 he taught at the [[University of Virginia]], after which he moved to [[Yale University]]. At Yale, he became the Philip  Schuyler Beebe Professor of Mathematics, and chaired the mathematics department for ten years. He was also a member of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], which he visited in 1933, 1938, and 1953.<ref>[http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/users/4684 Hedlund, Gustav A., Institute for Advanced Study]</ref> He was the Director of [[Institute_for_Defense_Analyses#Center_for_Communications_and_Computing|IDA's Communications Research Division]] in Princeton 1962-1963.<ref name="leibler">{{cite journal|journal=The Institute of Mathematical Statistics Bulletin|volume=18|number=6|year=1989|pages=581|title=Letter to the editor: Center for Communications Research|author=David I. Lieberman|url=https://ufdc.ufl.edu/AA00070316/00106/71}}</ref>
He retired from Yale in 1972, but afterwards held a visiting professorship at [[Wesleyan University]].<ref name="citation"/><ref name="briscoe"/>

Hedlund died in 1993.<ref name="briscoe"/> He has over 200 [[academic genealogy|academic descendants]], many of them through two of his students at Virginia, [[Walter Gottschalk]] and W. Roy Utz, Jr.<ref name="mg"/>

==Research==
One of Hedlund's early results was an important theorem about the [[ergodicity]] of [[geodesic flow]]s.<ref>[http://www.projecteuclid.org/DPubS?verb=Display&version=1.0&service=UI&handle=euclid.bams/1183501760&page=record ''Dynamics of Geodesic Flow.''] In: ''Bulletin of the AMS.'' vol. 45, 1939.</ref> He also made significant contributions to [[symbolic dynamics]], whose origins as a field of modern mathematics can be traced to a 1944 paper of Hedlund, and to [[topological dynamics]].<ref name="citation"/><ref name="briscoe"/>

The [[Curtis–Hedlund–Lyndon theorem]], a topological characterization of [[cellular automata]], is named after Hedlund. Hedlund first published this theorem in 1969, crediting [[Morton L. Curtis]] and [[Roger Lyndon]] as co-discoverers.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Hedlund | first = G. A.
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01691062
 | issue = 4
 | journal = Mathematical Systems Theory
 | pages = 320–375
 | title = Endomorphisms and Automorphisms of the Shift Dynamical Systems
 | volume = 3
 | year = 1969| s2cid = 21803927
 }}.</ref>

Hedlund was the co-author of the book ''Topological Dynamics'' (with [[Walter Gottschalk]], American Mathematical Society, 1955).<ref>Review of ''Topological Dynamics'' by Y. N. Dowker, {{MR|0074810}}.</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Halmos, Paul R.|authorlink=Paul Halmos|title=Review: ''Topological dynamics'', by W. H. Gottschalk and G. A. Hedlund|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.|year=1955|volume=61|issue=6|pages=584–588|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1955-61-06/S0002-9904-1955-09999-3/S0002-9904-1955-09999-3.pdf|doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1955-09999-3|mr=1565733|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Hedlund was elected to [[Sigma Xi]] in 1943.<ref>{{citation|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=TA4tAAAAIBAJ&pg=5606,2895285|title=Sigma Xi Elects Eleven Persons To Membership|journal=The Cavalier Daily|date=April 21, 1943}}.</ref>

In 1972, a conference on topological dynamics was held to honor Hedlund on the occasion of his retirement from Yale. The editor of the [[festschrift]] from the conference, [[Anatole Beck]], wrote that it was "our token of respect to the man who did so much to foster and build this field".<ref>{{citation
 | editor-last = Beck | editor-first = Anatole | editor-link=Anatole Beck
 | doi = 10.1007/BFb0061716
 | location = Berlin
 | mr = 0370654
 | publisher = Springer-Verlag
 | series = Lecture Notes in Mathematics, Vol. 318
 | title = Proceedings of the Conference on Topological Dynamics held at Yale University on August 23, 1972, in honor of Professor Gustav Arnold Hedlund on the occasion of his retirement
 | year = 1973| volume = 318 | isbn = 978-3-540-06187-8 }}.</ref>
